Firm History
J. Harry Covington and Edward B. Burling opened the doors of Covington & Burling in Washington, DC, on January 1, 1919. The eminent George Rublee soon joined them as a partner, and a former Brandeis clerk named Dean Acheson was hired two years later as an associate. The firm was off and running.
One of the firm's first cases was an international arbitration in The Hague, with Burling and Acheson representing the Kingdom of Norway in the Norwegian Shipowners proceeding against the United States. Success in that arbitration—an award of the then-astronomical sum of $12 million—helped build the firm's reputation. The burst of New Deal legislation a decade later increased corporate demand for regulatory expertise, leading the firm to gain recognition in fields ranging from economic to product regulation.
The firm steadily grew during the 1930s, eventually becoming known as Covington, Burling, Rublee, Acheson & Shorb. The lengthy name had its uses, as an old New Yorker piece recounted in describing how the firm's name helped someone who was "groggy trying to dig up enough names for a litter of puppies that just arrived." Notwithstanding the five mythical puppies, several years later the firm's name was restored to Covington & Burling.
The 1940s saw the coming of age of a legendary group, including Tommy Austern (a master in fields ranging from antitrust to food and drug law), Gerhard Gesell (a litigator later renowned as a federal judge), Dan Gribbon (the brilliant trial and appellate lawyer who became the firm's leader in the 1970s), Charlie Horsky (a pioneer in bankruptcy and other areas whose range was reflected by his pro bono representation of Fred Korematsu), and Howard Westwood (the iconoclast who hummed the "Internationale" in the firm's hallways during the 1930s and served as a Drill Instructor on Parris Island during World War II).
After the war’s conclusion, the firm boomed. Together with a wide array of regulatory disciplines, antitrust litigation became one of the staples of the firm's practice. But there was plenty of variety. Westwood and Stan Temko played a major role in the Steel Seizure case. Acheson, now back from his service as Secretary of State, teamed with the young Brice Clagett and successfully represented Cambodia in its border dispute with Thailand. Hugh Cox, later described by Justice Harlan as "the perfect advocate," was distinguishing himself at the Supreme Court bar.
In 1960, with Peter Hutt's arrival, the firm was 100 lawyers strong. By the end of the 1960s, the firm's growth required a move to 888 16th Street, just across Lafayette Park from the White House. The firm's tangible and enduring commitment to pro bono was also sealed during the late 1960s with the firm's launch of its still-running lawyer rotation program at a Neighborhood Legal Services office. The firm, an early leader among law firms in terms of religious tolerance, had begun to diversify in other ways as well. In 1974 and 1975, Virginia Watkin and Wes Williams became the firm's first woman and African American partners. Led by Horsky, armies of lawyers toiled on the Penn Central reorganization throughout most of the 1970s.
Lawyer headcount topped 200 around 1980, and it was again time for a larger home. In 1981, the firm became the first major non-governmental tenant on the Pennsylvania Avenue corridor, moving to a new building at 1201 Pennsylvania Avenue. Another generation of stars came into its own, including Michael Boudin (appellate standout and later appellate judge), Peter Nickles (a competitive tri-athlete and later the District’s Attorney General), Chuck Ruff (who started the firm's white collar practice and later impressed the nation as President Clinton's White House Counsel during the impeachment trial), Bob Sayler (who almost single-handedly created a new field of practice called insurance coverage), and Paul Tagliabue (who left to become the NFL’s Commissioner and is once again our colleague).
With this new generation of leaders, the 1980s and 1990s were decades of growth and expansion. In 1988, C&B opened a London office, followed by a Brussels office in 1990. Even bigger moves came in 1999, when Covington opened its first West Coast office in San Francisco and brought on board a 60-lawyer New York City firm called Howard, Smith & Levin, which boasted a remarkably similar value system and first-rate practices. 2008 literally and figuratively involved opening new doors. We launched our Beijing office, and then we expanded our intellectual property practice with the addition of approximately 50 lawyers who joined us in Washington and San Francisco and helped us start a new office in Palo Alto.
On January 20, 2009, President Obama was inaugurated, and we said farewell to a number of our lawyers who answered his call to service. Among them was our partner Eric Holder, who became the Attorney General of the United States almost sixty years to the day after Dean Acheson’s swearing in as Secretary of State.
In 2012, Covington became one of the first U.S. law firms to open an office in Seoul. A few months later, the firm opened an office in Shanghai. At the end of 2014, the firm’s Washington office moved to CityCenter, anchoring the first mixed-use development in the heart of downtown. In 2015, we welcomed Eric Holder back to the firm as a partner, opened a new office in Los Angeles, and brought on board a large government contracts practice group in Washington. In 2017, the firm added fully integrated global project finance and development capabilities, which included opening new offices in Dubai and Johannesburg. Covington opened a new office in Frankfurt, Germany in 2018 as the firm's third European office. In 2023, the firm opened a new office in Boston, adding Covington's sixth U.S. location.
Now in our tenth decade, the firm's good work and good works have continued. Today, the firm numbers more than 1,600 lawyers and advisors in 14 offices. Those lawyers and their practices are extraordinarily diverse, obviously more so than at the firm's creation more than 100 years ago. But importantly, the traditions handed down by the firm's founders—excellence, tolerance, integrity, and a commitment to public service and professionalism—endure today.

Morrison Foerster transforms complexity into advantage. With our collective intelligence, we shape powerful legal strategies that move your business forward while living our shared values.

We solve your most critical multidimensional challenges in a way that provides clarity around the risk you are facing and gives you confidence in your chosen path. Our Values
MoFo Chairs
Eric is the Chair of Morrison Foerster.
Eric has been a trusted advisor on hundreds of public and private M&A, private equity, and financing transactions over the course of his career. As part of his market-leading M&A practice, he counsels strategic acquirers and targets in a variety of industries, including technology (semiconductors, software, AR/VR, fintech, AI), healthcare, consumer products, financial institutions, media, gaming, and transportation. He represents leading U.S. and global companies and regularly advises on complex cross-border transactions.
Eric is regularly recognized by leading publications, including The Legal 500 US and Chambers USA, with client sources describing him as “greatly skilled at advising on the most complex and high-profile M&A transactions” and noting that he “combines strong technical skills and a flair for complexity with commercial awareness, pragmatism and sound judgment.”
Larren Nashelsky served as the chair of Morrison Foerster from 2012 to 2022, before retiring in July 2023. As chair, he oversaw a period of phenomenal success for the firm, driven by the strategic needs of the firm’s clients. Today, MoFo is a global powerhouse, translating our litigation and transactional experience and talent into client success.
During Larren’s leadership, the firm’s global footprint expanded, with new offices opened in Berlin, Boston, Singapore, Miami, and Austin. Through it all, the firm remained true to its unique culture and values. Larren was dedicated to continuing and building on MoFo’s proud legacy of leadership in inclusion and engagement. Similarly, he was committed to advancing pro bono and community service work, which are part of MoFo’s DNA.
Prior to serving as chair of MoFo, Larren served as a firmwide managing partner and founded and led Morrison Foerster’s Business Restructuring + Insolvency Group.
Keith Wetmore served as chair of Morrison Foerster from 2000 to 2012, and as chair emeritus from 2012 to 2017, before moving on to another leadership role outside of the firm. During his tenure, he took the lead in setting policy and providing strategic direction to the firm. Under Keith’s leadership, the firm expanded internationally and in the United States in key financial and technology centers, and was ranked on The American Lawyer A-List for nine consecutive years.
Before becoming chair, Keith led the firm’s 50-lawyer Finance and Infrastructure practice, bringing to his engagements 20 years’ experience in debt and lease finance, both domestic and international. He represented money center banks as agents in syndicated credit facilities, including multibillion-dollar working capital and acquisition financings, as well as smaller transactions, with particular emphasis in the technology and forest products sectors.
Steve Dunham served as Chair of Morrison Foerster from 1996 to 2000.
Peter Pfister served as chair of Morrison Foerster from 1993 to 1997, with responsibility for all aspects of the firm’s professional, strategic, and financial decisions. In leading the law firm during a challenging economic downtown, Peter helped preserve Morrison Foerster’s progressive culture—including its longstanding commitment to pro bono work and its professional values—while improving the state of the firm’s finances. As the San Francisco Daily Journal reported of his leadership, “Peter proved to be the leader of character and integrity that Morrison needed.”
Before becoming chair of the firm, Peter served as a managing partner from 1990 to 1993, responsible for coordinating all practice areas in the firm’s 14 offices at the time. From 1986 to 1990, he served as chair of Morrison Foerster’s firmwide Litigation Department. After stepping down as chair, Peter served for many years as one of the firm’s general counsel. In that capacity and until he retired in 2020, Peter was called upon as Morrison Foerster’s Dispute Resolution Partner to resolve issues relating to all aspects of the firm’s practice.
Peter’s litigation practice included antitrust, securities, intellectual property, and professional liability actions.
Carl Leonard served as Chair of Morrison Foerster from 1984 to 1993.
Marshall Small served as chair of Morrison Foerster from 1982 to 1986, and in 1996 became the firm’s first general counsel, a title he held until 2013. Marshall joined the firm in 1954 and was the first Jewish lawyer hired by the firm. Over the next 40 years, Marshall became a preeminent leader in corporate and securities law. Marshall was elected to the partnership in 1961 and went on to hold numerous leadership positions, including managing partner from 1971 to 1976.
Marshall represented what is best about Morrison Foerster and was instrumental in creating the partnership culture we have today. He was an outstanding mentor to all who worked with him. It was more than a technical mastery of his field that attracted both partners and associates to his office for consultation. Marshall championed the importance of inclusion and was dedicated to pro bono work, including a case where he was appointed by the U.S. Supreme Court to protect the rights of a San Quentin prisoner.
Marshall was with the firm for 65 years and was one of the most important people in the history of Morrison Foerster.
Robert Raven served as Chair of Morrison Foerster from 1978 to 1982.

The MoFo Legends video series brings to life the stories of individuals who have played a defining role in shaping Morrison Foerster’s legacy. Their experiences offer a window into the lives of lawyers and business professionals whose work—in practice and in service—continues to inspire us.

Kræfterne skal bruges klogt, hvis vi skal møde de behov for forandring, vores samfund står overfor. Vi ruster aktører til at arbejde og samarbejde for at skabe nye løsninger på svære problemer. Vi hjælper med at mobilisere og motivere forandringsledere, der kan vise de nye veje.
Ændr mindset og adfærd
Forandring kalder på, at vi mennesker ændrer vaner og ser andre perspektiver. Vi skaber kreative og strategiske koncepter, der kan ses og mærkes. Som ændrer menneskers syn på verden, og flytter deres adfærd.
Flyt dagsordner og politik
Politiske beslutninger, meningsdannelse og offentlig debat kan fremme og hæmme forandring. Vi sætter ind og skaber aftryk på tværs af medier og arenaer, hvor politiske beslutninger modnes og træffes. Vi sikrer, at de vigtige perspektiver, budskaber og viden er med, når forandring skabes.
Styrk purpose og lederskab
Virksomheder og organisationer bør være medskabere af de store forandringer. Til gavn for dem selv og for alle. Vi finder den position, hvor kerneforretning og purpose mødes i en højere enhed. Vi former en relevant stemme, som vækker genklang og skaber bevægelse.

På grund af stor interesse for forrige event afholder vi endnu et Breakfast Academy om, hvordan organisationer, virksomheder og lobbyister bedst påvirker den politiske dagsorden – på de digitale platforme.
Den virtuelle samtale er stadig en undervurderet mulighed for at massere meningsdannelsen samt påvirke politikere og embedsmænd.
Så hvordan gør man? Hvilke fælder skal man undgå, og hvilke vinderformler kan vi grave frem? Hvem er de bedste, de hurtigste og de stærkeste på digitale platforme?

Der er mulighed for at stille spørgsmål, og så stiller vi som altid kaffe og morgenmad frem.

Breakfast Academy: Partnerskaber | Operate
Retrieved via http: https://operate.dk/breakfast-academy-partnerskaber
Kom med til vores morgenmøde og bliv klogere på partnerskaber.
Partnerskaber er helt essentielle for at finde holdbare løsninger på de komplekse samfundsproblemer, vi står overfor. Ligestilling, energieffektivisering, ulighed i sundhed, integration . Alligevel går det galt fra tid til anden. Nu har du chancen for at blive klogere på, hvornår partnerskaber fejler, og hvad du kan gøre for at få dem til at lykkes.
Partnerskaber. Partnerskaber. Partnerskaber. Du hører det igen og igen. Regeringen snakker om “strategiske partnerskaber” for milliarder. Verdensmål 17 siger det. Alle fonde og projektorganisationer med respekt for dem selv siger det.
Alligevel tænker du måske. Der er jo så meget, der kan gå galt? Og det er der!
Du kan risikere, at det skader din organisations image, hvis indsatsen fejler, eller jeres partnere træder ved siden af. Du kan ende med at bruge uanede mængder af timer og ressourcer på koordinering i stedet for at komme ud af starthullerne. Du og dine partnere kan ende med at blive ”ufrivillige” modstandere og spænde ben for hinanden.
Ja, du kan simpelthen miste kontrollen.
Listen af gode grunde til at lade være er altså stor. Partnerskaber kan ærligt talt være lidt af et problembarn, og man fristes til at tænke, at det måske er nemmere bare at fikse det alene?
Men problemet med den tanke er bare, at det sjældent virker!
Vi kan ikke være ambitiøse på de komplekse problemers vegne alene . Skal de faktisk løses kræver det samarbejde. Det kræver, at vi organiserer os i partnerskaber.
Ingen sidder nemlig alene på løsningen af de komplekse problemer. Det kalder på, at vi arbejder sammen og mødes på tværs af sektorer, greb og erfaringer. Det kalder på filantropi, myndigheder, erhvervsliv og civilsamfund.
Med andre ord. Der er ingen vej uden om!
Vi vil heldigvis gerne hjælpe dig på vej.
Til Breakfast Academy fortæller vi om de største faldgruber, de gode greb og hvordan du bedst indtager rollen som partnerskabsleder. Kort fortalt, vi guider dig til at forvandle et potentielt problembarn til et vaskeægte ønskebarn.
Udover best-practice tips og egne erfaringer, får vi besøg af et hold skarpe eksterne oplægsholdere, der deler deres indsigter, gode råd og erfaringer med partnerskaber. Du kan blandt andet opleve:
- Judith Kyst , Direktør hos Madkulturen - Claus Blomgreen , Backbone-leder hos MedVind i Østerbyen - Tine Larsen, Backbone-konsulent hos MedVind i Østerbyen - David Harrington , Co-Director hos United for Brownsville

WHAT WE DO
Results & Value
First things first: We get results.
But that is not all we are about. Our passion — what drives us above and beyond — is doing all of that and adding value every step of the way.
What does that mean?
Value is a slippery concept. The definition varies from client to client and industry to industry. Here’s how we see it.
There are no cookie-cutter solutions. Even with seemingly routine matters, we take time to listen to clients, to hear and understand what’s important to them, to craft solutions tailored to their businesses and aligned with their cultures, and to do it all in an efficient, cost-effective and transparent manner. Our goal is to leave clients wondering why all service providers don’t deliver more than they expected. More proactive thinking. More diverse views. More attentive service. More innovative approaches. More connections. More bang for the buck. More value.
Here’s why. Beating client expectations requires significant investment in our business and in our clients’ businesses. We have to assemble, nurture and deploy the talent, the tools, the technology, and the techniques to make it work.
We’ve made the necessary commitments. We invest in listening to our clients directly and through third-party interviews that deliver the unvarnished skinny on our performance and how we can continuously improve our service delivery.
We invest in client and industry teams that help us understand your world as if we were in your shoes.
We invest in systems and technologies including cutting-edge AI tools, that render us more efficient and more effective.
We have mastered the customization of alternative fee arrangements with an array of proven alternatives to the billable hour across matters of all sizes and shapes. That’s why the firm earned top rankings in the PERSUIT 50 and took first place for our use of innovative pricing models. We invest in pro bono partnerships, programs to advance diversity and inclusion in the profession, secondments, and much more.
Most firms talk a good game when it comes to value. But there’s a reason we have been on BTI Consulting’s Client Service A-Team top 30 list — the gold standard — 19 times. And there’s a reason Financial Times continuously ranked us one of the most innovative law firms in North America.
WHEN WE COMMIT
Insights & Industries
If we believe something is right for our clients — whether that’s entering a new market, bringing in useful technology, hiring a talented lateral, or upgrading our associate training — we go for it. Our commitment to industry teams is a good example.
We are true believers in taking an industry-centric approach to serving clients. Not because it’s the latest Big Law fad. Because we decided, many years ago, that it makes sense. Clients are not focused on our business. They care about their own. That’s why our industry teams are central to how we serve them.
Lots of firms lay claim to an industry approach. But very few make the investments — in leadership, knowledge, support — needed to succeed. Clients have long made it clear that, other than price-of-admission factors such as expertise and responsiveness, nothing is more important to them than outside counsel knowing their business. And believe it or not, their business is not M&A or class actions or e-discovery. They are in the energy business, the banking and finance business, the healthcare business. Our industry teams pave the way for more efficient and effective service by viewing the world through our clients’ eyes. With more than a dozen teams, we are one of the few — and first — firms to look at the law from a business perspective.
There’s another reason industry focus matters. We are a uniquely collaborative law firm. Our lawyers and consultants like and respect one another. It is second nature to them to share insights across sectors. This enables us to “see around corners” and let clients know that important changes afoot in one sector may soon find their way to another. Our clients tell us such insights are invaluable, and we agree. We have taken purposeful steps, through our industry team program, to assure that our legal counsel is informed by a commercial mind-set.
History
Egbert R. Watson, private secretary to President James Monroe, launches a practice in Charlottesville, Virginia — the seed that will blossom into McGuireWoods.
George Perkins joins Watson in what will become predecessor firm Perkins, Battle & Minor.
Murray Mason McGuire starts a practice in Richmond that becomes the partnership of McGuire & Bryan.
The modern firm is born when the Battle and McGuire firms join to form McGuire, Woods & Battle.
A merger spawns McGuire, Woods, Battle & Boothe, adding Virginia offices in Alexandria, Charlottesville, Norfolk, Richmond and Tysons, plus Washington, D.C.
Offices are added in Baltimore and Jacksonville.
The firm launches a public affairs subsidiary, McGuireWoods Consulting.
Offices are added in New York, Chicago, Atlanta, Charlotte and Pittsburgh.
McGuireWoods merges with Ross and Hardies, adding 155 lawyers.
The firm expands to California through a 40-lawyer merger in Los Angeles.
Renowned IT firm Gordon & Glickson joins McGuireWoods in Chicago.
The firm completes a major merger with 145-lawyer Helms Mulliss & Wicker, with offices in Charlotte and Raleigh.
The firm opens a London office via a merger.
The firm enters the Texas market with offices in Austin and Houston.
The firm opens in Dallas, its third Texas office.
Through a combination with innovative litigation boutique Integer Law, the firm expands its California presence.
The firm opens an office in San Francisco.
The firm enhances its service to clients with interests in Asia through a strategic alliance with FuJae Partners in Shanghai.

F&B advisory is a specialist consulting service that helps developers, owners, investors and hospitality operators shape the commercial, operational and experiential role of food and beverage within a project.
It can include market research, F&B strategy, concept planning, brand positioning, operator recommendations, feasibility analysis, revenue modelling and long-term performance planning.
For hotels, mixed-use developments, destinations, food halls, retail environments and urban districts, F&B advisory helps ensure that restaurants, cafés, bars and hospitality spaces are planned around real market demand, commercial viability and guest experience.
TGP International’s F&B advisory service supports clients across the full strategic planning process, from early-stage feasibility through to concept development, operator strategy and commercial planning.

F&B market and demand analysis

Strategic recommendations for hotels, destinations, food halls, mixed-use developments and hospitality-led assets
Our role is to help clients understand what F&B should do within a project, how it should be structured and how it can support long-term commercial performance.
F&B can have a significant impact on how people use, value and remember a place. Well-planned restaurants, cafés, bars and hospitality spaces can support footfall, dwell time, guest satisfaction, leasing appeal, brand perception and overall asset performance.
Without a clear F&B strategy, developments risk creating spaces that are difficult to lease, poorly matched to local demand, operationally inefficient or commercially underperforming.
F&B advisory helps ensure that the right formats, concepts, operators and commercial models are considered early, so food and beverage become a strategic driver of value rather than an afterthought.
F&B master planning defines the role, scale, location and mix of food and beverage within a development or destination.
It looks at how restaurants, cafés, bars, food halls, kiosks, grab-and-go formats, hotel F&B, event catering and other hospitality uses should be distributed across a site.
A strong F&B master plan considers customer behaviour, footfall patterns, spatial planning, commercial targets, operational requirements, market gaps and the wider positioning of the asset.
The aim is to create the right balance of everyday convenience, destination dining, social experience and commercial performance.
TGP assesses F&B demand through a combination of research, benchmarking, market intelligence and project-specific analysis.
This may include reviewing the local competitive landscape, consumer behaviour, spend patterns, tourism drivers, residential and office populations, catchment dynamics, existing supply, category gaps and relevant food and beverage trends.
We then translate this insight into practical recommendations on concept mix, pricing, positioning, brand selection, operational requirements and commercial opportunity.
Where required, we also work with local subject matter experts to validate strategy against cultural context, market maturity and location-specific guest expectations.
Yes. TGP works with clients to integrate F&B strategy into mixed-use developments, urban districts, retail schemes, cultural destinations, hotels, entertainment assets and large-scale placemaking projects.
In these environments, F&B is not only about individual restaurants or cafés. It plays a wider role in shaping the rhythm of the place, supporting day-to-night activity, encouraging repeat visits, creating social value and strengthening the identity of the destination.
Our advisory work helps ensure F&B is connected to the wider commercial, spatial and experiential strategy of the development.
F&B feasibility and revenue modelling help test whether a proposed F&B strategy is commercially viable.
This can include revenue forecasting, sales assumptions, cover projections, spend-per-head estimates, operating model considerations, rent assumptions, category performance, space productivity and scenario analysis.
The objective is to help developers, owners and investors understand the potential commercial performance of different F&B options before committing to detailed design, leasing or operational decisions.
F&B advisory should ideally be involved at the earliest concept, feasibility or master planning stage.
Early involvement allows the F&B strategy to influence site planning, unit sizing, back-of-house requirements, servicing, customer flow, tenant mix, leasing strategy and operational design.
Bringing F&B advisory in too late can create avoidable challenges, including inefficient layouts, unsuitable unit sizes, unrealistic revenue expectations or concepts that do not fully align with market demand.
Yes. TGP supports hotel owners, operators, developers and investors with F&B advisory for restaurants, bars, cafés, lounges, breakfast operations, banqueting, events, in-room dining and wider guest experience.
Hotel F&B needs to balance guest expectation, operational efficiency, brand identity and commercial return. Our advisory work helps hotels assess what their F&B offer should be, how it should perform and how it can better support the overall asset.
This may include concept strategy, operational review, revenue optimisation, positioning, guest journey analysis, brand partnerships and recommendations for improving underperforming F&B spaces.
Yes. TGP International works across global markets, with experience in Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Asia.
Our advisory approach is adapted to each market, taking into account local culture, consumer behaviour, tourism patterns, development context, operational realities and commercial maturity.
This international experience allows us to bring global hospitality insight while ensuring strategies are relevant to the local market and the specific needs of each project.
What makes TGP International’s F&B advisory approach different?
TGP combines strategic advisory with real-world hospitality, operational and brand development experience.
This means our recommendations are not only based on market research or commercial modelling. They are also shaped by an understanding of how restaurants, cafés, bars, hotels, food halls and hospitality destinations actually operate.
Our work is designed to be practical, commercially grounded and deliverable. We help clients move from high-level strategy to decisions that can influence leasing, design, operations, guest experience and long-term performance.

De transitie van het landelijk gebied is in volle gang. Nederland kent een grote verscheidenheid aan natuur en landschappen, waarbij de sterke verwevenheid met functies, met name die van natuur met de landbouw, uniek is. De kwaliteit van ons landelijk gebied staat onder druk. En dat is zorgelijk, want in het landelijk gebied ligt de oplossing voor een aantal complexe vraagstukken die spelen op het gebied van onder andere water, natuur, klimaat en biodiversiteit.
Het belang van verduurzaming en klimaatadaptatie maakt (her)ontwikkeling van industriële locaties complexer dan ooit. Organisaties krijgen te maken met allerlei uitdagingen op het gebied van veiligheid, milieu of wet- en regelgeving. Op dit soort momenten wilt u als industriële organisatie kunnen vertrouwen op diepgaande inhoudelijke en procesmatige kennis, zodat u zeker bent van continuïteit en werkt aan een toekomstbestendige locatie.
Steden staan niet stil. De energietransitie, een klimaat adaptieve inrichting, de druk op de woningmarkt en mobiliteitsopgaven leggen flinke claims op de schaarse ruimte in stedelijke gebieden. Tegelijkertijd willen we de kwaliteit van de leefomgeving verhogen door meer groen aan te leggen en de CO2-uitstoot te verminderen. Het zijn bijzonder mooie en complexe uitdagingen.

Nu de Europese Unie strenge milieurichtlijnen heeft opgesteld en de vraag naar groenere alternatieven blijft groeien, verschuiven de onderwerpen waarmee u rekening moet houden bij investeringen, fusies en overnames. Duurzaamheidsambities waarmaken
In het dynamische bedrijfslandschap is duurzaamheid uitgegroeid van een stip op de horizon tot een belangrijke motor voor blijvend succes. De inzet van de Europese Unie voor de Green Deal-ambities is vastgelegd in een nieuw Sustainable Finance Framework met de SFDR (Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation), CSRD (Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive) en EU Taxonomy als belangrijke pijlers. Om te voldoen aan deze ingrijpende regelgeving is het belangrijk een deskundige partner aan uw zijde te hebben, die u kan helpen bij het navigeren door deze richtlijnen en bij het bereiken van uw duurzaamheidsdoelen.
Het strategische belang van duurzaamheid
Nu het wereldwijde streven naar duurzaamheid wetgeving verandert en innovatie aanwakkert, krijgt u als belegger te maken met een toenemend aantal beslissingsfactoren. De taak om risico's in te schatten, naleving te garanderen en een responsieve strategie te ontwikkelen is niet langer slechts een uitdaging – het is een noodzaak. Te midden van de complexiteit van klimaatadaptatie, circulariteit en biodiversiteit wordt de rol van ingenieursbureaus steeds belangrijker. Dat is waar het TRIS-team ( Transactions and Responsible Investment Services ) van TAUW als leidraad dient. Wij bieden meer dan alleen begeleiding; wij bieden u duidelijkheid.
Sustainable Finance Regulation Calendar 2026-2027
Onze Sustainable Finance Regulation Calendar voor 2026-2027 biedt u de belangrijkste deadlines en publicaties met betrekking tot de SFDR, EU Taxonomy, CSRD en andere wetgeving. Let op : de kalender is Engelstalig.
Bekijk de kalender
Duurzaamheid als basis voor duurzame groei
Wanneer u bijvoorbeeld wilt investeren in vaste activa of wanneer u een fusie, overname of verkoop voorbereidt, is het niet langer voldoende om alleen naar de traditionele milieu- en veiligheidsrisico's te kijken. Duurzaamheidsrisico's en -kansen met betrekking tot klimaatmitigatie, klimaatadaptatie, biodiversiteit en circulariteit vormen in toenemende mate risico's en kansen waarmee u rekening moet houden. Inzicht in de werkelijke impact van deze duurzaamheidsuitdagingen op uw specifieke bedrijf of target is essentieel. Evenals zicht op welke acties u dient te ondernemen en welke investeringen u moet doen en wanneer, met behoud van uw financiële en operationele vermogen.

Concrete strategieën om duurzaamheidsdoelen te bereiken
Onze experts beschikken over het technisch inzicht om uw duurzaamheidsambities te vertalen naar praktische strategieën. Of het nu gaat om het ontrafelen van de ingewikkelde regels van SFDR, CSRD of het vakkundig doorgronden van de EU Taxonomy, wij begeleiden u van complexiteit naar zekerheid. Samen zetten we duurzaamheid om in concrete bouwstenen voor succes. Tijdens dit gezamenlijke traject stellen we u in staat om ambitie te transformeren naar actie en uw visie te vertalen naar meetbare resultaten. Werk samen met ons aan een toekomst waarin uw investeringen niet alleen in overeenstemming zijn met de regelgeving, maar ook met uw visie op duurzame groei.

Als wirtschaftlich, organisatorisch und fachlich unabhängiges Unternehmen erarbeiten wir tragfähige, nachhaltige und zukunftsorientierte Lösungen für unsere Auftraggeber.
Als einer der führenden Schweizer Anbieter für Dienstleistungen im Bereich Geologie und Geotechnik ist es unser Anliegen, nicht nur trotz sondern gerade wegen qualitativ hochwertiger Arbeit die wirtschaftlichste Lösung für unsere Kunden zu finden.
Unser fundiertes Know-how ist dabei nicht nur der Bonus unserer Kunden. Wir investieren konsequent in die Ausbildung unserer Mitarbeitenden und unsere Infrastruktur und bieten damit ein attraktives und abwechslungsreiches Wirkungsfeld.
Zudem befindet sich unser gesamtes Aktienpaket im Besitz von Mitarbeitenden. Dies garantiert für unsere wirtschaftliche Unabhängigkeit

Google's Chrome Gets a Major Security Boost with Data Loss Prevention Features - Teknita
Retrieved via http: https://www.teknita.com/googles-chrome-gets-a-major-security-boost-with-data-loss-prevention-features/
Blog
Home / Resources / Blog Post
Google has recently announced six new features for its Chrome browser that aim to enhance the security and privacy of enterprise users. These features include data loss prevention (DLP), protections against malware and phishing, and the ability to enable zero-trust access to the search engine.
Data loss prevention (DLP)
DLP is a set of policies and tools that help prevent unauthorized access, use, or transfer of sensitive data. Google has added three new DLP features for Chrome that extend beyond its existing DLP capabilities:
Context-aware DLP: This feature allows administrators to customize their DLP rules based on the security posture of the device being used. For example, admins can allow users to download sensitive documents if they are accessing them from a corporate device that is up to date on security patches or has endpoint protection software installed. However, the feature will block users from downloading sensitive documents on personal devices or devices that do not meet the security criteria.
URL filtering: This feature allows administrators to block or warn users about visiting websites, or categories of websites, that breach the organization’s acceptable use policies. For example, admins can restrict access to popular file sharing websites, while still allowing file sharing via the corporate file-sharing site.
DLP for print: This feature allows administrators to stop users from printing files that contain confidential data.
Extension security
Extensions are small programs that add functionality to the browser. However, some extensions may pose risks to users or request permissions that are not aligned with the organization’s policies. Google has added two new features for Chrome that help assess and manage extension security:
Extension risk assessment platforms: Google has integrated two browser extension risk assessment platforms, CRXcavator and Spin.AI Risk Assessment, into Chrome Browser Cloud Management. These platforms provide risk scores for extensions based on various factors such as permissions, code quality, privacy practices, and more. Administrators can view the risk scores of the extensions being used in their browser environment and take appropriate actions.
Browser security event notifications: Google has added two new browser security event notifications for Chrome that alert IT and security teams when an extension is installed or when a browser crashes. These notifications can help jumpstart investigations and identify potential threats or vulnerabilities.
Zero-trust access
Zero-trust access is a security model that assumes no trust between users and resources, and requires verification for every request. Google has enabled zero-trust access for Chrome through BeyondCorp Enterprise, its zero-trust solution. BeyondCorp Enterprise provides continuous authentication and authorization for users and devices accessing web applications and services. It also offers protection against malware and phishing attacks by isolating risky web sessions in a secure sandbox.
Google’s new features for Chrome are designed to help enterprise users work securely and productively on the web. By implementing advanced DLP and gaining more visibility into extension security and critical security events, organizations can reduce the risk of data loss and take a more proactive approach to cybersecurity.

Disasters can strike at any time, whether it’s a natural disaster, a cyberattack, or a human error. When your critical systems go down, you can lose revenue, productivity, and customer trust. That’s why you need a reliable disaster recovery (DR) solution that can help you restore your operations as quickly as possible.
But traditional DR solutions can be costly and complex to manage. You need to maintain a secondary site with redundant hardware, data center space, and staff. You also need to ensure that your data and applications are always up-to-date and ready to failover in case of an emergency.
That’s where cloud-based DR solutions come in. Cloud-based DR solutions use software to replicate your workloads, data, and system settings to the cloud. In the event of a disaster, you can spin up your cloud-based replicas as a secondary production site and keep your business running until your primary site is back online.
One of the best cloud-based DR solutions available today is Carbonite® Recover for Google Cloud Platform (GCP). Carbonite® Recover is a disaster recovery as a service (DRaaS) solution that reduces the risk of unplanned downtime by securely replicating your critical systems to the Google Cloud Platform. With Carbonite® Recover, you can benefit from:
Recovery times measured in minutes and recovery points measured in seconds, reducing the risks of lost productivity and revenue
Easy deployment and management of your DR solution through a single console
Cost savings by eliminating the need for a physical secondary site and paying only for what you use in the cloud
Confidence in your data protection strategy with non-disruptive, self-service tests, failover reports, and professional services support
Carbonite® Recover works with any physical, virtual, or cloud-based system and supports various platforms such as Microsoft Windows, Linux, VMware, Hyper-V, and more. You can also choose from different replication modes such as continuous replication for near-zero data loss or scheduled replication for less critical systems.
With Carbonite® Recover for GCP, you can leverage the scale, availability, and security of Google’s cloud infrastructure. You can also take advantage of Google’s global network of regions and zones to ensure optimal performance and compliance.

Imagine a small start-up from Eastern Europe entering a world dominated by players with huge budgets and a global reach. That’s precisely the story of Bene Meat Technologies, a start-up with a vision to produce cultivated meat at an affordable price. The world’s leading media are writing about the company today. How did we manage to build a global reputation for this start-up?
We started working on Bene Meat Technologies’ media image in Czech Republic from scratch in 2021. The key to success was a carefully thought-out, fact-based strategy, transparent communication and respect for business know-how. We also presented the personalities at BMT and showed unique ways of leading the work and the team. Our aim was to show the public and the media that something unique is being created in the Czech Republic.
A major breakthrough came in 2023, when Bene Meat Technologies obtained official EU registration for the production of cultivated meat as a pet food ingredient. This groundbreaking event caught the attention not only in Czech media but in the European continentand global media as well. Reuters, The Guardian, Stern, The Financial Times and other major global titles, including those in the veterinary, pet food and food businesses, have written about the company’s success. With this breakthrough, Bene Meat Technologies rose to the level of a global player, and we used a targeted PR strategy to ensure that the whole world heard about it.

=== PAGE: Karel Schwarzenberg | https://www.amic.cz/en-GB/case-studies/Karel-Schwarzenberg
Public farewell to Karel Schwarzenberg at the Church of the Knights of Malta | AMI Communications
Retrieved via http: https://www.amic.cz/en-GB/case-studies/Karel-Schwarzenberg
Karel Schwarzenberg, former minister of foreign affairs, presidential candidate and descendant of a famous noble family, died on 12 November 2023, leaving the Czech Republic without one of the few publicly and politically active figures of whom it could be proud in an international context.
It was not very well known, but Karel VII of Schwarzenberg, like his ancestors, was a proud member of the Sovereign Order of Malta. It is a Catholic order whose main mission has been to help those in need for 900 years. In the Czech Republic, the knights carry out charity work through Maltese Aid, a publicly beneficial organization that AMI Communications has been helping with communication pro bono for 10 years.
The moment the family of Karel Schwarzenberg approached the Sovereign Order of the Knights of Malta about the public part of the farewell taking place in the order’s church in Prague, it was clear that such an event would become the subject of huge media attention. And because the Knights of Malta are focused on charity rather than media relations, they needed a partner to help them make things happen in an organized and dignified manner, to everyone’s satisfaction.
Therefore, the order’s representatives approached our agency with a request to provide a complete press service, which included keeping the media informed, organizing them on site, representation on camera, creating information panels and many other activities.
In just a few days, AMI learned the fascinating history and family ties of the Schwarzenberg family, as well as its centuries-long association with the Knights of Malta. And because no mistakes can be made in such an event, we went full speed during the pre-Christmas period. This time, however, the biggest challenge was not to get the information to the media, but to protect some of the information and give it to the media at the right time.
However, guiding the media and public through such an important (and sad) event was, above all, a huge honour and we will never forget the three days spent in the Church of the Knights of Malta.
AMI arranged:
Professional and well-organized communication with media and partners, commensurate with the importance of the event.
Complete press service including representation on camera.

=== PAGE: die durchfuehrung einer risikoinventur f | https://severn.de/portfolio/die-durchfuehrung-einer-risikoinventur-fuer-eine-renommierte-privatbank
Die Durchführung einer Risikoinventur für eine renommierte Privatbank - Severn Consultancy
Retrieved via http: https://severn.de/portfolio/die-durchfuehrung-einer-risikoinventur-fuer-eine-renommierte-privatbank
Kunde & Anforderung
Die Anforderung „bisher unbekannte Risiken zu identifizieren“ gilt als zentrales Element der MaRisk Novelle 2010 und stellte für unseren Mandanten aufgrund ihrer Komplexität eine große Herausforderung dar.
MaRisk AT 2.2 Risiken
Die Anforderungen des Rundschreibens beziehen sich auf das Management der für das Institut wesentlichen Risiken. Zur Beurteilung der Wesentlichkeit hat sich die Geschäftsleitung regelmäßig und anlassbezogen im Rahmen einer Risikoinventur einen Überblick über die Risiken des Instituts zu verschaffen (Gesamtrisikoprofil). Die Risiken sind auf der Ebene des gesamten Instituts zu erfassen, unabhängig davon, in welcher Organisationseinheit die Risiken verursacht wurden. […]
Die Durchführung einer angemessenen Risikoinventur erfordert zudem die Verknüpfung der identifizierten Risiken mit den Ertrags- und Vermögenskennzahlen des Instituts. Damit ist ein methodisch ausgereiftes Vorgehen und die Implementierung bzw. Anpassung adäquater Risikomanagementprozesse zwingend erforderlich.
Eine fehlende Methodik, knappe interne Ressourcen sowie ein sehr kurzer Implementierungszeitraum bildeten somit die Grundlage einer vertrauensvollen, effizienten und nachhaltigen Zusammenarbeit mit Severn.
Zielsetzung
Aus dem von Severn entwickelten Konzept zur Durchführung einer MaRisk konformen Risikoinventur resultierte das Gesamtrisikoprofil des Institutes.
Auf Grundlage zahlreicher Gespräche mit Marktteilnehmern und Regulatoren bezüglich der verschärften aufsichtsrechtlichen Anforderungen stellte Severn ein umfassendes Konzept zur Durchführung einer Risikoinventur zur Verfügung.
Der Vorteil dieses Konzeptes ist, dass vor allem die Geschäftsbereiche, die einen hohen Wertbeitrag für das Unternehmen liefern, in das Risiko-Assessment eingebunden werden. Somit wird ein Bezug zur aktuellen Ertrags- und Vermögenssituation hergestellt.
Die in enger Zusammenarbeit mit den Geschäfts- und Fachbereichen erarbeiteten Resultate der Risikoinventur wurden problemlos in die Reporting- und Steuerungsprozesse der Bank integriert, um Schwachstellen und Umsetzungsmaßnahmen an das Top Management zu adressieren.
Vorgehensweise
Durch die frühzeitige Einbindung der Geschäfts- und Fachbereiche wurde eine ganzheitliche Akzeptanz der Ergebnisse sowie der Umsetzungsmaßnahmen sichergestellt.
Für die einzelnen Geschäftsbereiche wurden individuelle und standardisierte Fragebögen von Severn zur Verfügung gestellt, die es den Bereichsleitern ermöglichten mit geringem Zeitaufwand die aktuelle sowie die perspektivische Qualität Ihrer Werttreiber zu bewerten. Um die Ressourcen des Mandanten zu entlasten, übernahm Severn die gesamte Koordination im Rahmen des Projektmanagements.
Die beantworteten Fragebögen wurden durch ein eigens von Severn entwickeltes Analyse-Tool ausgewertet und graphisch aufbereitet. Gemeinsam mit den Geschäfts- und Fachbereichen wurden die Ergebnisse in konstruktiven Workshops besprochen sowie für aufgedeckte Schwachstellen Mitigationsmaßnahmen formuliert. Die frühzeitige Einbindung aller Bereiche sicherte die sehr hohe Akzeptanz der durchgeführten Risikoinventur.
Ergebnisse und Kundennutzen
Die Anforderungen des Mandanten wurden durch die Leistungen von Severn zur vollsten Zufriedenheit erfüllt. Unter starkem Zeitdruck gelang es dem Team von Severn eine effiziente Risikoinventur umzusetzen sowie die entsprechenden Prozesse zu etablieren.
Darüber hinaus gelang es Severn im Rahmen des entsprechenden Budgets:
…stets flexibel und bedarfsorientiert auf die häufig volatilen Rahmenbedingungen einzugehen.
…einen reibungsfreien Dialog zwischen Risikocontrolling und den involvierten Markt- und Marktfolgebereichen sicherzustellen.
…eine hohe Akzeptanz der gesamten Risikoinventur bei den involvierten Geschäftsbereichen – dank frühzeitiger Einbindung und hoher Transparenz – zu erzielen.
…das Analyse-Tool bzw. das entsprechende Know-How in die Linie zu übergeben.
…die Methodik und die Ergebnisse in das bestehende RisikomanagementFramework des Kunden (u.a. Entwicklung einer Gesamtrisikomatrix) zu integrieren.

=== PAGE: fraud quick check fuer eine renommierte  | https://severn.de/portfolio/fraud-quick-check-fuer-eine-renommierte-privatbank
Fraud-Quick-Check für eine renommierte Privatbank - Severn Consultancy
Retrieved via http: https://severn.de/portfolio/fraud-quick-check-fuer-eine-renommierte-privatbank
Bestehende Instrumente genügen nicht den neuen strengen rechtlichen Vorgaben
Mit der Individualität und Vielfältigkeit des renommierten Bankhauses steigt gleichermaßen die Verantwortung, die individuellen Geschäftsprozesse den immer strengeren regulatorischen Anforderungen anzupassen.
Die Einhaltung rechtlicher Vorgaben ist unverzichtbar, um die angesehene Reputation der Privatbank – vor allem gegenüber den anspruchsvollen Kunden – nicht zu gefährden. Zunehmend verschärfte aufsichtsrechtliche Anforderungen – wie bspw. die des neuen § 25 c KWG – erhöhen darüber hinaus die Notwendigkeit, das interne Risikomanagement speziell auf die Verhinderung von betrügerischen Handlungen auszurichten.
§ 25c KWG
[…] Institute haben im Rahmen ihrer ordnungsgemäßen Geschäftsorganisation und des angemessenen Risikomanagements zur Verhinderung von betrügerischen Handlungen zu ihren Lasten interne Grundsätze und angemessene geschäfts- und kundenbezogene Sicherungssysteme zu schaffen und zu aktualisieren und Kontrollen durchzuführen. […]
Risikoorientierung ist das Schlagwort bevorstehender Prüfungshandlungen. So wird eine Risikobetrachtung von der Aufsicht erwartet, die häufig über die bereits durchgeführten Gefährdungsanalysen hinausgeht.
Bestehende Instrumente des klassischen Risikomanagements genügen kaum noch dem gewachsenen Druck, genau die Betrugsrisiken zu erkennen, die das Institut an vielfältiger Stelle gefährden.
Die Kenntnis über diese Risiken ist allerdings notwendig, um zielgerichtet Maßnahmen ableiten zu können. Nur so können wirtschaftskriminelle Handlungen erkannt werden, bevor diese entstehen und über Jahre hinweg geschaffene Unternehmenswerte bedrohen.
Erste risikoorientierte Betrachtung von Betrugshandlungen
Allein der umfassende Blick der Compliance Funktion innerhalb der Bank reichte nicht aus, um die Gefahren von wirtschaftskriminellen Handlungen auch bis in die letzten Organisationsbereiche hinein richtig einzuschätzen. Eine Lösung war erforderlich, die der Bank schnell und verlässlich den erforderlichen Überblick über die Gefahren aus Betrugshandlungen verschafft.
An dieser Stelle halfen die Erfahrungen von Severn in der Geldwäsche- und Betrugsprävention für Banken. Genau diese sollten dazu beitragen, die Risiken im Institut zu erkennen und spezifische Präventions- und Sicherungsmaßnahmen abzuleiten.
Bestehende Kontrollmaßnahmen sollten insofern verbessert werden, um Betrugsdelikte künftig schneller zu erkennen und frühzeitig zu verhindern.
Fraud-Quick-Check offenbart bisher verborgene strukturelle Schwächen
Erst die enge Einbindung von Experten der verschiedenen Abteilungen des Bankhauses ermöglichte es, organisatorische oder technische Schwachstellen zu identifizieren, die bisher verborgen blieben. Jedem Bereich wurde somit geholfen, sich mit dessen konkreten Gefahrenpotentialen aus wirtschaftskriminellen Handlungen aktiv auseinanderzusetzen.
Mittels der von Severn eingebrachten Checklisten war es erstmals für die Bank möglich, nicht nur bestehende Verfahren zu prüfen. Auch Aussagen zum Umsetzungsstand der neuen aufsichtsrechtlichen Vorgaben an die Betrugsprävention konnten getroffen werden.
Durch strukturierte Experteninterviews wurden mit der Risikoeinschätzung innerhalb nur weniger Tage die Gefahren für das Institut transparent. Auf Basis der vorgefundenen Schwachstellen wurden konkrete Präventionsund Sicherungsmaßnahmen abgeleitet und in einem fundierten Maßnahmenkatalog zusammengefasst.
Gleichzeitig wurden bereits einzelne Quick Win‘s erfolgreich umgesetzt und somit eine Effizienzsteigerung von bestehenden Kontrollmaßnahmen schon während der Projektdurchführung erreicht.
Leistungen
Die bewährte Methodik von Severn stellt bestehende Strukturen auf den Prüfstand
Grundlage für die zeitgerechte Realisierung des Fraud-Quick-Checks war eine bewährte Methodik von Severn, einschließlich eines fundierten Toolsets. Fundierte Checklisten wurden an das Bankhaus angepasst und machten so eine Beurteilung von bestehenden Verfahren möglich.
Daneben trug die Vorbereitung und Moderation der Experten-Interviews wirksam dazu bei, Schwachstellen zu identifizieren und eine möglichst objektive Einschätzung der Risikosituation vorzunehmen. Darauf aufbauend wurden – ergänzend um die Erfahrungen von Severn – Präventionsmaßnahmen zielgerichtet abgeleitet und bestehende Kontrollsysteme verbessert.
Severn unterstützte weiterhin die Kommunikation auf Unternehmens- und Vorstandsebene und konnte somit erstmalig ein Bewusstsein für diese Art von Risiken in der Organisation verankern.
Darüber hinaus stellte die revisionssichere Aufbereitung der Analyse- und Auswertungsergebnisse einen ersten Nachweis für die Etablierung eines risikobasierten Ansatzes im Umgang mit Betrugsrisiken gegenüber Aufsicht und Wirtschaftsprüfern dar.
Präventivmaßnahmen nur da, wo auch Risiken das Institut bedrohen
Auf Basis der durchgeführten Einschätzung von Betrugsrisiken konnte der Bank ein auf die wirklichen Gefahren abgestimmter Maßnahmenkatalog mit spezifischen Empfehlungen an die Hand gegeben werden.
„Maßnahmen fokussieren sich nunmehr auf die konkreten Risikobereiche und werden nicht nach dem „Gießkannenprinzip“ verteilt. Das erhöht die Wirksamkeit und spart gleichermaßen kostbare Ressourcen“, erklärt Norman Nehls, verantwortlicher Senior Manager für die Durchführung des Fraud-Quick-Checks.
Innerhalb des Privatbankhauses stellt nunmehr die Betrugsprävention eine aktive Disziplin dar. Mit dem Fraud-Quick-Check wurden potenzielle Gefährdungen in den einzelnen Abteilungen erhoben und damit ein „Bewusstsein“ für diese Risiken geschaffen. Mit einem abgestimmten Präventionskonzept kann nun schneller und flexibler da reagiert werden, wo die Betrugsrisiken am höchsten sind.
Durch eine Optimierung bestehender Präventionsmaßnahmen und Kontrollkonzepte wurde die Effizienz der Organisation als Ganzes erhöht, ohne Ressourcen für neue umfassende Aufgabenbereiche zu binden. Mehrere Schultern tragen künftig dazu bei, die Betrugsprävention in der gesamten Organisation stetig zu verbessern.
Gleichermaßen erfüllen die Ergebnisse die verschärften aufsichtsrechtlichen Anforderungen und dienen zugleich als Ausgangspunkt für eine Umsetzung eines konzernweiten Anti-Fraud-Managements.
„Mit dieser für unser Bankhaus ersten Auseinandersetzung mit den Risiken aus Betrugshandlungen haben wir es geschafft, bestehende Sicherungsmaßnahmen zu optimieren und unsere Kontrollstruktur erheblich zu verbessern. Gleichzeitig fühlen wir uns nunmehr gut genug aufgestellt, um internen wie auch externen Prüfungen sicher zu begegnen.“ so der Leiter der Compliance-Abteilung und verantwortlicher Projektleiter des Bankhauses.

Amidst that, modern brands and businesses have to do more than simply conjure an image. They must make an impact. Brands today have a unique opportunity to deliver on that promise—one that lives through modern marketing at the intersection of creativity and effectiveness. Our experts are focused on their pursuit of delivering brand impact for our clients throughout the entire creative process, from strategy to execution.

Our Team
Laurent Ezekiel
Laurent Ezekiel is a recognized leader known for leveraging the transformative power of creativity, not just to solve complex challenges and drive significant business impact, but to actively shape the very future of marketing for the world's most iconic brands. As Global CEO of The Ogilvy Group, he leads one of the world's most iconic creative networks, driving seamless solutions woven at the intersection of its diverse marketing capabilities, spanning advertising, PR, social & influence, customer engagement, consulting, and health. This expansive tapestry of talent includes award-winning creative powerhouses like DAVID, Grey, INGO, NCA, thjnk, and Village Marketing.
Since joining WPP in 2019, Laurent has proven his exceptional ability to assemble world-class talent and deliver creative impact at an unprecedented scale. Most recently, he served as CEO of WPP Open X, spearheading a multi-agency, multi-disciplinary team that serves as the global marketing partner for The Coca-Cola Company. WPP Open X masterfully integrates creative, media, social, influencer, commerce, PR, data and technology into a cohesive marketing ecosystem that is innovative at its core and unprecedented in its scale. This global network-to-network partnership was specifically designed to support The Coca-Cola Company’s marketing transformation, covering more than 200 brands in 195 countries and to be a catalyst for marketing innovation and excellence.
Under Laurent’s strategic direction, WPP Open X developed and scaled innovative solutions such as Studio X and harnessed the collective creative power of the company’s agencies to propel Coca-Cola to become Brand of the Year at the 2024 Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity.
Laurent previously spent 16 years at Publicis Groupe holding various leadership roles including President of North America & International at Digitas. He started his career at Saatchi & Saatchi and went on to work at Grey London.
Beyond his commercial achievements, Laurent is deeply committed to making a positive impact. He holds a Master’s in Environment & Development, reflecting his dedication to WPP’s sustainability efforts. He has also served on the WPP’s Global Inclusion Council, championing new programs that foster a respectful culture where every individual feels a sense of belonging and can thrive.
Laurent’s global perspective is rooted in his upbringing as half-French, half-Indian in London, a city he still calls home alongside New York. He is a proud father of three, a passionate supporter of Arsenal FC, and a fiercely loyal Coke Zero customer.

Ann Garreaud
As Ogilvy's Global Chief Financial Officer, Ann Garreaud oversees all financial and commercial operations across the agency's global network and serves as a member of parent company WPP’s finance leadership team. She is a distinguished financial leader, renowned for her deep understanding of the evolving agency landscape and unwavering focus on client value. Prior to her appointment at Ogilvy, Ann dedicated 25 years to Publicis Groupe, notably as EVP of Global Client Finance & Business Solutions, where she led financial and commercial operations for their Global Client Practice, driving significant growth and transforming business models. Her Publicis tenure also includes global CFO roles for Publicis Health and Publicis Worldwide.
Earlier in her career, Ann served as the U.S. CFO for the joint ventures between Y&R and Dentsu. She holds a BA from Lehigh University and an MBA from the Gabelli School of Business at Fordham University. Ann is recognized for her strategic leadership and commitment to leveraging financial expertise to deliver exceptional value and innovative solutions for clients.
Horacio Genolet
Horacio is Chief Executive Officer of Ogilvy LATAM & CEO of WPP Creative LATAM and has led Ogilvy’s Latin American operations since January 2017.
Under Horacio’s leadership, Ogilvy Latin America has been recognized by Cannes Lions as Latin America Regional Network of the Year for four consecutive years, earning its latest designation in 2022.
Horacio joined Ogilvy in 1993 in Argentina as an Account Supervisor. He was soon promoted to Account Group Director where he oversaw clients such as Duracell, IBM, SmithKline-Beecham and Mercedes Benz. After a three-year stint as Advertising Manager at Telecom Group, the largest cellular telephone company in Argentina, Horacio moved to media agency Carat as Regional Director for Latin America.
In 2004 Horacio returned to Ogilvy in Mexico as VP of Client Services in charge of accounts such as American Express, Volvo, Coca-Cola and Gillette.
In 2006, he was appointed as Managing Director of the Ogilvy Miami, while also taking over duties as Regional Account Director for American Express, Motorola, Kraft and Lenovo. Horacio returned to Ogilvy Mexico in 2008 as Executive VP and in August of 2011 he was appointed CEO.
Under his stewardship, Ogilvy was ranked the number one agency in Mexico by Merca2.0 for three consecutive years (2014, 2015, 2016).
Horacio has been recognized for five consecutive years (2012-2017) as one of the 300 Most Influential Leaders of Mexico by Líderes Mexicanos magazine, and he was also named one of the Top 100 Marketing and Advertising Leaders by Merca2.0.
In 2015, Horacio became President of the Executive Board of the Mexican Association of Advertising Agencies. In 2016, he acted as President of the EFFIE Awards Council.
Horacio has a degree in Advertising from the Universidad del Salvador in Buenos Aires and a Master's Degree in Integrated Communications from Bonn University in Germany.
Fiona Gordon
Fiona is the Global CEO of Advertising, where she drives the evolution of Ogilvy’s advertising, brand, and content capabilities to meet the shifting needs of clients. Since joining Ogilvy as a graduate trainee in the 1990s, she has held leadership positions across EMEA, Asia, and the US. Prior to her current role, she served as CEO of Ogilvy UK from 2021, where she led the agency to become WARC’s #1 creative agency in the UK in 2024. Her leadership spurred notable new business wins, such as Molson Coors and Valeo Foods, and multiple industry recognitions, including the Financial Times’ ranking of Ogilvy Consulting as a top consulting firm and the Global Influencer Marketing Awards’ Best Large Influencer Marketing Agency title. Fiona’s prior roles include Chief Client Officer for Ogilvy EMEA and WPP UK Team Lead for Walgreens Boots Alliance, where she secured strong business results and the brand’s highest reputation scores in a decade. She was also Group Chairperson of Ogilvy Singapore from 2011-2015, leading the agency to accolades like SE Asia Agency of the Year and SE Asia Agency Head of the Year. Throughout her career she has led accounts including Unilever, American Express, GSK, Singtel, and Mondelēz. An active industry leader, she is on the Advisory Board of Stella (WPP’s Women’s Network), the IPA Council, WACL, and the American European Business Association, and co-chairs the Creative and Cultural Action Group for Make London a Living Wage City. In 2021, she was named to Ad Age’s Leading Women list.

Kappie Kopp
Kappie Kopp is Global Head of Communications for The Ogilvy Group, where she leads the agency's worldwide communications strategy, safeguarding and elevating Ogilvy's global reputation while championing its creative product, capabilities, and talent across all brand channels.
With nearly 20 years of experience anchored in creative agency leadership and brand-building, Kappie specializes in the fusion of rigorous communications strategy and cultural storytelling . Her core focus is on the vital role communication plays in shaping a company’s strategic decisions and how those decisions shape people’s relationships with brands— ultimately building the infrastructure of trust that enables co mpanies to move with clarity and impact.
She was promoted to her current role after serving as Senior Vice President, Creative Communications at Ogilvy, where she built a first-of-its-kind storytelling infrastructure to elevate the agency's creative reputation and led day-to-day communications for North America, one of Ogilvy's largest markets.
Prior to Ogilvy, Kappie held practice leadership roles at MSL and LEWIS, working across healthcare, B2B tech, energy management, and consumer industries, and led PR and communications for multiple Publicis agencies, including Leo Burnett and Arc Worldwide. Before entering the agency world, she spent a decade at SCAD: The University for Creative Careers, driving communications and special initiatives through a period of major institutional growth — operationally, programmatically and e conomically .
Outside of work, Kappie cherishes time with her family. An avid runner and reader, she also enjoys puzzles, cooking, and working in the garden.
Mick McCabe
Mick is a thinker and proven leader who works at the intersection of strategy, creativity, and technology to create impact and growth for Ogilvy and its clients. As Global Chief Strategy Officer, Mick leads a team of 1,500+ strategists across the Ogilvy network to deliver world-class, insights-driven creative solutions for clients.
Mick joined Ogilvy from Publicis Groupe where he held various leadership roles over the past decade, including Global Chief Strategy Officer for Publicis Worldwide and CSO roles for Le Truc, Publicis Creative USA, and Leo Burnett. During his tenure at Publicis, he worked extensively on the group’s largest accounts, including Allstate, Bank of America, CVS, Heineken, Samsung, and Walmart. Altoids, BMW, Nintendo, Ikea, and McDonald’s are other marquee brands he has helped advise over his career.
Prior to Publicis, Mick led strategy teams at Deutsch and Kirshenbaum Bond. Additionally, Mick served as a strategic advisor and acting CMO for the launch of the world's biggest VR fitness platform, Supernatural, which in 2020 won Fast Company’s Best Innovation and Time Magazine’s Best Invention awards. His work has been recognized by Cannes, Jay Chiat Awards, and includes two Grand Prix Effies.

Questions we get before a first call.
A project controls consultancy provides the disciplines that keep complex programmes on track: planning and scheduling, cost management, risk management, and integrated reporting. SOMA does this for UK infrastructure programmes across rail, highways, nuclear, water, defence and energy — either as a stand-alone capability (for example, running a quantitative risk analysis) or as an embedded controls team.
Quantitative risk analysis is a Monte Carlo simulation of a project's cost and schedule risks. It produces a confidence range — typically P50, P80 and P95 outcomes — rather than a single number. A QRA lets a board or sponsor decide how much contingency to approve at a defensible confidence level, and identifies the top risks driving that exposure. SOMA delivers QRA to AACE International recommended practices (57R-09, 113R-20, 118R-21, 123R-22) using Safran Risk, Primavera Risk Analysis, @Risk or Acumen Risk.
SOMA is a pure-play project controls firm, not a side-line of an audit, tax or general management-consultancy practice. We do not run graduate-led teams, we do not sell controls as a staff-augmentation commodity, and we do not write reports in consultant-speak.
SOMA was founded in 2024 by Adam O'Neill. The team is chartered through the APM, ACostE, AACE (DRMP and EVP), RICS and IRM, with more than a decade of project controls experience each on UK infrastructure programmes.

Project management is the overall discipline of delivering a project — scoping, team leadership, stakeholder management, decision-making, and day-to-day running. Project controls is the analytical spine that supports those decisions: planning and scheduling, cost management, risk analysis, earned value, and integrated reporting. A project manager runs the project; the controls function gives them the data to run it well. On major UK programmes the two are distinct roles, often held by different people, working alongside one another.

=== PAGE: about | https://0711.net/about/
About | 0711
Retrieved via http: https://0711.net/about/
Die Geschichte von ist wie eine kurze Geschichte des deutschen HipHops.
Wie alles begann...
Eigentlich wollten Schowi und Strachi nur ’ne gute Party schmeißen. 1996 im Prag. „0711 Club“ wurde die Eventreihe getauft. Hätte man den beiden damals gesagt, dass daraus eines der bekanntesten Kreativnetzwerke Deutschlands wird, hätten sie vermutlich die Augen verdreht und den nächsten Flyer gedruckt. Und genau das haben sie getan. Flyer auf Flyer. Abend auf Abend. Bis der 0711 Club das Wohnzimmer der HipHop-Szene wurde. Freundeskreis, Afrob, Massive Töne und alle Stars der Szene – sie gaben sich hier die Klinke in die Hand. Plötzlich war Rap salonfähig, die Majors klopften an, aus Leidenschaft wurde Business. Für die Jungs von 0711 war klar: Wenn wir das jetzt machen, dann machen wir’s richtig.
Stuttgart = Hauptstadt
Die Szene war das Fundament. Jetzt brauchte es vier Wände drumherum. So wurde das 0711 Büro gegründet. Ein Ort, an dem sich die Community selbst organisierte, ohne sich dabei zu verlieren. Was dann folgte, war Stadtprägung. Events überall, gleichzeitig, nonstop. Flyer, die wie Trophäen gesammelt wurden und ein Name, der als Gütesiegel galt. Wenn 0711 draufstand, kamen die Leute. Was heute Cultural Marketing heißt, war hier einfach Alltag. Die Höhepunkte dieser Ära? Das HipHop Open. MTV. Internationale Strahlkraft. Stuttgart auf der Karte. Für immer.
Same roots. More branches.
Mit wachsendem Netzwerk kam die Erkenntnis: Da steckt mehr drin. Brands merkten, dass 0711 Türen öffnen konnte, die kein Media-Budget der Welt aufschließt. Also wurde gebaut. Neue Leistungen, neue Units. 0711 Livecom für Live Communication und Eventmanagement. 0711 Digital für digitale Kommunikation und Influencer Marketing. 0711 Talents für die Aktivierung von Talents in der Markenkommunikation. 0711 Entertainment: eigener Merchandise, lokale Aktivierungen und Szene und Stadtgeschehen. Alles unter einem Dach, alles mit derselben DNA. Das nächste Kapitel einer Geschichte, die 1996 mit einem Flyer begann.
Vom HipHop-Hobby zum Agentur­netzwerk
30 Jahre später
Noch immer Stuttgart. Noch immer dieselbe Haltung. Das Netzwerk ist gewachsen, die Leistungen breiter, die Projekte größer – aber das Warum? hat sich nie verändert. Weil wir Teil der Community bleiben wollen, die 0711 groß gemacht hat. Weil wir Subkulturen für schützenswert halten. Weil wir Brands und Kultur so zusammenbringen möchten, dass beide davon profitieren. Und weil wir ab und zu eine verdammt gute Party schmeißen wollen.
Am 23.05.26 haben wir unser Jubiläum groß gefeiert. Mit allen langjährigen Wegbegleiter:innen, über 6.500 Gästen und einem 2,5h Konzert auf dem Stuttgarter Schlossplatz. Darüber hinaus gibt es die SWR Doku „0711 – HipHop made in Stuttgart“ sowie den Podcast „Mutterstadt 0711 – HipHop-Hauptstadt Stuttgart!?!“ . Schaut und hört rein, was in 30 Jahren 0711 alles passiert ist!
Das ist heute

Embedded four weeks inside Neighborly's in-house creative team. Turned the repetitive work behind 19 home-service brands (resizes, US to Canada versions, seasonal edits, briefs, color checks) into eight documented AI workflows the team now runs on its own.
Neighborly is the parent company behind 19 home-service brands, Mr. Handyman and Molly Maid among them, across the US and Canada. All that creative runs through one lean in-house design team. Five to seven requests a day, 400-plus last quarter, much of it the same work in a different size.
The graphic designer carried the highest-volume tickets: display and banner resizes for every placement, plus US and Canada versions of each campaign, often 40-plus assets from one request. The associate creative director had already built a ChatGPT script that spits out 68 print templates from a dropdown, and still spent her days hunting for files across systems.
AI was in the building. Everyone used it a little, each from a different starting point, and the first passes kept coming back off-brand. The tools started blank every time, with no idea what Gotham Bold or a brand's exact blue looked like.
So the engagement ran four weeks, embedded role by role. Find the highest-leverage repetitive work, build its AI workflow on a live ticket, document it for anyone to run, and leave the team running without me.
The operating principle went up on day one: stop starting from zero, start from one.
Every session ran on a real ticket. A Mr. Handyman trifold needing new copy. Three social graphics needing the same photo swapped in, and (the fun one) a stock house photo that needed fall, 10 p.m., and string lights along the trim. If a workflow couldn't survive the actual request, it didn't get documented.
The Keep/Change prompt formula became the spine: say exactly what to touch and what to leave alone, then name the output you want. Around it, the habits that make the model behave: four options instead of one, a fresh chat per job, the model writing and fixing its own prompt. All written down so a new hire with zero AI experience gets the same result.
The guardrails went in before the builds. Talent contracts restricting changes to a person's likeness got a hard line, and anything touching brand marks was staged behind legal. Then I specced the permanent fix for the off-brand first pass: a brand-context layer, one ChatGPT project per brand holding its guidelines, font files, logos, color values, and a few approved examples, so every edit starts on-brand.
GPT Image 2.5 shipped midway through week two. The playbook was re-tested and rewritten around it that same week, every original step preserved.
Eight workflows documented and tested on Neighborly tickets, with five more scoped and staged. Copy changes on a finished layout in one pass. US to Canada versions from one prompt (the Canadian logo, the .ca URL, neighbourly with a u). One photo into five sizes, all five landing. Seasonal and holiday edits off one base photo, four options at a time, plus photo swaps across a batch of graphics and transparent cutouts of the brand elements models like to mangle. Weekly reporting straight off the monday.com export. And a color-guide QA workflow that reads about 60 swatches across all 19 brands and cross-checks the CMYK values against four models before a vehicle-wrap printer sees them.
Brief assembly, the creative PM's bottleneck at 15 to 60 minutes per request and about eight requests a day, dropped to under a minute. Raw form data in, formatted brief out.
It all lives in a shared Notion hub (step-by-step documentation, copy-paste prompts, session recordings) built to survive turnover. The creative director owns adoption now, and the graphic designer who opened the month saying AI wasn't her first instinct closes tickets with it by default.
The last session, a lunch and learn for a dozen people on the wider marketing team, gave the habits somewhere to spread. Four weeks in, the design team runs it without me.

About Our Team and Firm
We founded Interline Technologies in 2018 in the San Francisco Bay Area, and we continue to serve our customers from here, along with a team that's distributed across the United States.
Principals
Drew Dara-Abrams Ph.D. is a co-founder and Principal at Interline Technologies. At Interline, Drew manages the firm's consulting engagements and product development. Drew's previous experience spans both industry and academic labs in transportation and geography.
His experience in industry includes serving as Head of Mobility Products for the Mapzen division of Samsung. While at Mapzen, he recruited and managed a team to build the Transitland open transit data platform, develop a worldwide routing/trip-planning engine, and build a global system to derive road traffic speeds from GPS data for The World Bank. Previously, Drew served as Chief Technology Officer for Kinnexxus, Inc. where he and his colleagues completed two successful Small Business Technology Transfer (SBIR) grants from the National Institutes of Health. He's developed and managed web applications serving upwards of millions of users, and has provided strategic, technical, and statistical consulting to major corporations, universities, and start-ups.
Drew holds a Ph.D. in computational geography from the University of California, Santa Barbara, and co-authored two textbooks, Supporting Web Servers and E-Commerce & Internet Law , published by Prentice-Hall.
Ian Rees Ph.D. is a co-founder and Principal at Interline Technologies. At Interline, Ian leads engineering and operations efforts, building and maintaining open data pipelines to power publicly accessible trip planners, accessibility analysis, and data validation for Interline’s clients.
Prior to Interline, Dr. Rees was a software engineer at Samsung’s Mapzen division and technical lead of the Transitland project, an effort to create an open, user-contributed, user-editable, fully validated repository of all public GTFS data in the world. Previous to Samsung, Ian held postdoctoral positions at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and Baylor College of Medicine, where he administered a data center and developed an online platform for biological imagery analysis.
Ian holds a B.S. in Biochemistry from the University of Houston, and a Ph.D. in Structural and Computational Biology from Baylor College of Medicine. Ian is proficient in several programming languages including Python, Ruby, and JavaScript, and is experienced building complex applications using PostgreSQL, Redis, Docker, Kubernetes, and all three of the major public clouds (Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud Platform, and Microsoft Azure).
